MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S RULE 60(a) MOTION TO CLARIFY
OR CORRECT ECF NO. 108
INTRODUCTION: THE ORDER IDENTIFIES THE ATTRIBUTED DECISION-
MAKER BUT NOT THE UNDERLYING ACTION
ECF No. 108 attributes to the District Judge a choice "to refrain from beginning any
discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss." ECF No. 108 at 2. The Order does
not identify the order, instruction, or other action on which that attribution rests. The District
Judge's docketed orders and notices address other subjects. The one earlier docketed order that
addresses discovery timing was signed by the previously assigned magistrate judge.
The same passage carries a second question of original meaning. Page 1 of the Order
identifies four requests: a scheduling order, a Rule 26(f) conference and discovery plans, an initial
pretrial conference, and a statement of the next scheduling event. ECF No. 108 at 1. Page 2 resolves
them through a statement about "any discovery." The Order does not state whether the attributed
1

choice was understood to reach the scheduling and planning steps it identifies, or substantive
discovery alone.
Plaintiff requests clarification of the action and scope the Court intended the passage to
describe, and correction of the text only if a qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended
ambiguity prevents the text from expressing that intent. Plaintiff seeks conformity between the
words of the Order and the determination the Court made on October 29, 2026. Plaintiff does not
seek a different determination.
II. RULE 60(a) PERMITS CORRECTION OF EXPRESSION, NOT
RECONSIDERATION OF AN INTENTIONAL DETERMINATION
A.
The Rule.
Rule 60(a) provides: "The court may correct a clerical mistake or a mistake arising from
oversight or omission whenever one is found in a judgment, order, or other part of the record. The
court may do so on motion or on its own, with or without notice." Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(a). The Rule
applies to an "order." This Motion invokes subdivision (a) alone. It does not invoke the grounds
for relief from a final judgment in subdivision (b).
B.
Sartin.
The Fourth Circuit has fixed the scope of subdivision (a). "Rule 60(a) is not confined just
to fixing typographical and other clerical errors." Sartin v. McNair Law Firm PA, 756 F.3d 259,
265 (4th Cir. 2014). A mistake arising from oversight or omission "occurs when there is an
inconsistency between the text of an order or judgment and the district court's intent when it
entered the order or judgment." Id. at 265-66. The phrase "also includes an unintended ambiguity
that obfuscates the court's original intent." Id. at 266. The power "is circumscribed by the court's
intent when it issued the order or judgment." Id. A court may not use the Rule to change its mind
about the determination it made. Id. at 265. Original intent "may be ascertained through
2

consideration of contemporaneous documents, such as a memorandum opinion or transcript, and
by the presiding judge's own subsequent statements regarding his intent." Id. at 266 (internal
quotation marks and citation omitted). The Fourth Circuit treated the issuing judge's subsequent
explanation as reliable evidence of that intent and examined whether the contemporaneous record
supported it. Id. at 266-67. The Fourth Circuit resolved the validity of an earlier Rule 60(a)
clarification order while deciding the causation element of a malpractice appeal. Id. at 263-67.
Two propositions follow. Original intent controls what correction is permitted. The issuing
judge's subsequent statement is evidence of that intent, assessed against the record.
C.
Chavez-Deremer.
The Fourth Circuit has also fixed the boundary. "[A] court is not authorized to use Rule
60(a) to reconsider an issue that has already been decided, or to revisit the court's decisions already
made." Chavez-Deremer v. Medical Staffing of America, LLC, Nos. 23-2176, 23-2284, slip op. at
69 (4th Cir. July 17, 2025) (published), reported at 147 F.4th 371, 416 (citing Sartin, 756 F.3d at
265). A party may not relabel a substantive ruling as a clerical mistake to obtain further litigation
of it. Id., slip op. at 69-70. The movant there sought further litigation of damages determinations
the district court had already made. Id. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the denial. Id., slip op. at 70-
71.
D.
The threshold applied.
The two decisions state one test. Rule 60(a) asks whether the words of the order express
what the issuing court intended when it entered the order. It does not ask whether the court should
have intended something else. This Motion asks the first question only.
The threshold carries an acknowledgment. An unexplained attribution is not necessarily an
inadvertent one. An omitted citation does not itself establish a correctable mistake. An intentional
inference is not a drafting error because it may be disputed. The Court "is not required to state
3

findings or conclusions when ruling on a motion under Rule 12 or 56 or, unless these rules provide
otherwise, on any other motion." Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)(3). This Motion does not rest on an
entitlement to additional reasons. If the passage accurately expresses the original determination
and contains no qualifying oversight, omission, or unintended ambiguity, Rule 60(a) requires no
expanded statement, and Plaintiff requests none. The Motion is directed to the possibility that the
passage does not express that determination, and to the means Rule 60(a) supplies if it does not.
E.
Presentation to the issuing magistrate judge.
ECF No. 108 disposed of two nondispositive case-management motions. A judge "may
designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine any pretrial matter pending before the court,"
subject to exceptions not relevant here. 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes
referral of such matters by entered order or on the instructions of a district judge. Rule 60(a) applies
to an "order." Correction of the Magistrate Judge's own nondispositive order to conform it to his
intent is presented to the officer whose intent governs. Plaintiff does not reopen the successor-
designation question through this Motion. That question is presented in ECF Nos. 97-99 and
remains pending there.
II. S THE IDENTIFIED RECORD DOES NOT RESOLVE THE ATTRIBUTION
Sartin identifies contemporaneous documents as one source of original intent. 756 F.3d at
266. The docketed orders and notices in this action that bear on the attribution are these.

Two distinctions follow from the table.
First, authorship. ECF No. 84 is the earlier docketed order that addresses discovery timing.
Magistrate Judge Davis signed it.
Second, content. ECF No. 84 describes the absence of a scheduling order and states that
discovery has not begun. It does not itself expressly identify a district-judge instruction postponing
discovery until the dismissal motions are adjudicated. A statement that a scheduling order has not
been entered is not the same statement as a description of a judge's decision not to enter one.
Neither distinction is offered to disturb ECF No. 84. Plaintiff's objections to ECF No. 84
are pending in ECF Nos. 89 and 90 and proceed on their own grounds. The distinctions serve one
purpose here. The reviewed documents do not identify the action ECF No. 108 describes.
5

The table does not exhaust every possible source of the attribution. Local Civil Rule 72
recognizes referral "on the instructions of a district judge." An instruction need not appear in a
separately entered order. The rule's text recognizes that method of assignment; it does not establish
that a particular discovery-postponement instruction existed or state its terms. Plaintiff does not
plead that no instruction existed. Plaintiff pleads that the reviewed record does not identify one
and that the passage does not state whether one exists.
IV.
ANY CLARIFICATION OR
CORRECTION MUST PRESERVE THE
ORIGINAL DETERMINATION
The passage may describe one of three things. The Rule 60(a) consequence differs for each.
An order or instruction of the District Judge.
If the Court intended the passage to describe an order or instruction the District Judge
issued, Plaintiff requests identification of that action as it existed when ECF No. 108 issued: by
date and docket citation where available, or by its operative terms where it was not separately
entered. Plaintiff requests only what is necessary to clarify the published description. Plaintiff does
not request chambers correspondence, drafts, internal deliberations, or testimony. If the existing
text describes the instruction accurately, no textual correction is warranted, and the clarification
identifies the action the Order already names.
B.
An inference or determination by the Magistrate Judge.
The posture on October 29, 2026 was three pending dismissal motions and no scheduling
order. If the Court intended the passage to state a conclusion it drew from that posture, rather than
a direction communicated by the District Judge, Plaintiff requests that the clarification say so.
Plaintiff does not request correction on that ground alone. Where the words express an intentional
inference, the words are accurate for Rule 60(a) purposes, and whether the inference is correct is
a question for a different procedural vehicle. See Chavez-Deremer, slip op. at 69. Correction is
6

warranted under this heading only if the words "the District Judge has chosen" do not express what
the Court meant when it wrote them.
C.
An inadvertent attribution.
If the identification of the District Judge, or the description of the source, resulted from
oversight, Rule 60(a) authorizes correction to identify what the Court actually intended. Sartin,
756 F.3d at 266-67 (concluding that the court did not abuse its discretion in using Rule 60(a) to
give effect to its original intent to sanction counsel individually, although its sanctions orders
named only "Plaintiffs"). Plaintiff proposes no replacement language. A substitute sentence would
state a determination the existing record does not establish. The Court must identify its original
determination before any replacement text can be settled.
V. CLARIFICATION SHOULD IDENTIFY THE ORIGINALLY INTENDED
REACH OF THE SAME PASSAGE
ECF No. 108 at 1 identifies the four requests before it: "First, Plaintiff requests entry of a
scheduling order. Second, Plaintiff requests an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f)
conference and file respective discovery plans. Third, Plaintiff requests an initial pretrial
conference. Fourth, if any of these steps are postponed, Plaintiff requests that the order state the
date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed." The underlying motions described their
own scope. ECF No. 103 sought "initial case management" and disclaimed any contention that
passage of the scheduling deadline "authorizes service of discovery." ECF No. 103 99 7-8. ECF
No. 105 sought "participation and reporting" and disclaimed any request for "answers to
interrogatories, production of documents." ECF No. 105 9 8.
The passage resolves those requests through a statement concerning "any discovery." That
treatment presents a question about the reach originally intended for the statement. Plaintiff does
not characterize the Order as inconsistent with itself. The Order can intentionally deny scheduling
7

and planning relief on the ground that substantive discovery has been deferred. Whether that
reasoning suffices is a reconsideration or review question and is not presented here. What is
presented is whether the words "any discovery" were intended to describe a decision about
substantive discovery alone, or a decision that also reached entry of a scheduling order, the initial
pretrial conference, the parties' Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report.
A related question of original operation attaches. Both motions were denied without
prejudice. That disposition is not unclear. The question is whether ECF No. 108 was intended only
to deny the requested orders, or also to recognize or direct a postponement of the planning steps
requested in ECF No. 105. The Order identifies "resolution of the pending motions to dismiss" as
the relevant event. ECF No. 108 at 2. The uncertainty concerns which steps the attributed decision
was understood to cover before that event occurs.
Plaintiff asks what the Order meant. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to enter a stay, to make
a good-cause finding, to decide any present deadline, to establish a resumption procedure, or to
rule that planning must proceed. Any clarification describes the Order's original operation. It does
not create a new postponement.
VI. THE LIMITED CLARIFICATION MATTERS WITHOUT DECIDING THE
MERITS
Accurate attribution distinguishes an order that implements a direction of the District Judge
from an order that states the Magistrate Judge's own inference or determination. Accurate scope
distinguishes denial of two requested orders from an intended direction concerning the planning
steps themselves. Each distinction concerns what the Order is, not whether the Order was right.
Plaintiff does not contend that every party's present obligations turn on this one sentence. Other
rules and orders may bear on them. Plaintiff contends only that the sentence should say what the
Court meant it to say.
8

This Motion does not argue that pending dismissal motions cannot support postponement.
It does not address the Rule 16(b)(2) date or the sufficiency of good cause. It does not challenge
the general proposition the Order quotes from another district court. ECF No. 108 at 1-2. Those
matters are reconsideration or review questions and are not presented here. This Motion does not
extend, and does not substitute for compliance with, the Rule 72(a) objection period applicable to
ECF No. 108.
VIl. CONCLUSION AND RELIEF
Plaintiff requests entry of the accompanying Proposed Order, which (1) to the extent
necessary to address a qualifying omission or unintended ambiguity, clarifies whether the passage
at ECF No. 108 at 2 describes an order or instruction of the District Judge, an inference or
determination by the Magistrate Judge, or another identified judicial action, and identifies any
order or instruction by date and docket citation or by its operative terms; (2) clarifies how that
action was understood, when ECF No. 108 issued, to relate to the scheduling order, the initial
pretrial conference, the Rule 26(f) conference, and the discovery-plan report, and whether ECF
No. 108 was intended only to deny the requested orders without prejudice or also to recognize or
direct postponement of the planning steps requested in ECF No. 105; (3) corrects the identified
passage by stating replacement language only if the existing text fails to express the determination
actually intended on October 29, 2026; and (4) leaves the denial without prejudice of ECF Nos.
103 and 105 unchanged, creates no new obligation, and resolves no separately filed application.

The Order attributes a decision to the District Judge and applies it to the requests before
the Court. Rule 60(a), as the Fourth Circuit construes it, permits the issuing judge to confirm that
the text expresses that determination and to conform the text if it does not. Plaintiff requests that
order, with the denial unchanged
